````json
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "e7fc257a3e9417f2",
    "text": "The stability of Earth's climate over billions of years has allowed life to evolve and diversify.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E10_Earth_as_a_Habitable_Planet.md",
    "document_id": "E10_Earth_as_a_Habitable_Planet",
    "sentence_index": 7,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "39f75e5f3841e8ba",
    "text": "The planet's diverse ecosystems, from rainforests to deserts, support a rich biosphere.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E10_Earth_as_a_Habitable_Planet.md",
    "document_id": "E10_Earth_as_a_Habitable_Planet",
    "sentence_index": 8,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "13a8c7a3377c707f",
    "text": "Earth's position in the \"habitable zone\" -- where water can exist as a liquid -- is a key factor in its ability to sustain life.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E10_Earth_as_a_Habitable_Planet.md",
    "document_id": "E10_Earth_as_a_Habitable_Planet",
    "sentence_index": 9,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "f5d2466652a53ed1",
    "text": "Overview of the Solar System",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E1_Overview_of_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E1_Overview_of_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 1,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "ed215f6fadf58840",
    "text": "Source: Wikipedia",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E1_Overview_of_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E1_Overview_of_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 2,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "78b927a9f05068c9",
    "text": "The Solar System is the gravitationally bound system of the Sun and the objects that orbit it.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E1_Overview_of_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E1_Overview_of_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 3,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "0ec7ee5e20d550ad",
    "text": "It formed about 4.6 billion years ago from the gravitational collapse of a dense region of a molecular cloud.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E1_Overview_of_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E1_Overview_of_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 4,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "11ab6f33aa228dc0",
    "text": "The collapse created the Sun at the centre, and the remaining material formed a protoplanetary disc from which the planets, moons, asteroids, and other bodies assembled.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E1_Overview_of_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E1_Overview_of_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 5,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "09a5fc3ba5246758",
    "text": "The Solar System consists of eight planets, five dwarf planets, and numerous smaller bodies.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E1_Overview_of_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E1_Overview_of_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 6,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "6bbc8498d38149a1",
    "text": "Over 99.86% of its mass is contained in the Sun.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E1_Overview_of_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E1_Overview_of_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 7,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "2f0d8e178e014b11",
    "text": "The four inner planets -- Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars -- are terrestrial (rocky) planets, while the four outer planets -- Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune -- are gas giants or ice giants.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E1_Overview_of_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E1_Overview_of_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 8,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "cf6d5f09ffa46eb3",
    "text": "Earth: The Third Planet from the Sun",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E2_Earth_The_Third_Planet_from_the_Sun.md",
    "document_id": "E2_Earth_The_Third_Planet_from_the_Sun",
    "sentence_index": 1,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "4fdcb5d8a0d4cba2",
    "text": "Source: Wikipedia",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E2_Earth_The_Third_Planet_from_the_Sun.md",
    "document_id": "E2_Earth_The_Third_Planet_from_the_Sun",
    "sentence_index": 2,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "5a8e0f09108ff3c4",
    "text": "Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the densest and fifth-largest of the eight planets.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E2_Earth_The_Third_Planet_from_the_Sun.md",
    "document_id": "E2_Earth_The_Third_Planet_from_the_Sun",
    "sentence_index": 3,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "3cbc03a1de4a90d7",
    "text": "It is the largest of the Solar System's four terrestrial planets.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E2_Earth_The_Third_Planet_from_the_Sun.md",
    "document_id": "E2_Earth_The_Third_Planet_from_the_Sun",
    "sentence_index": 4,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "83cdc6e4fa4d4d1a",
    "text": "Earth is the only known planet to have large amounts of liquid water on its surface, and it is the only astronomical object known to harbour life.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E2_Earth_The_Third_Planet_from_the_Sun.md",
    "document_id": "E2_Earth_The_Third_Planet_from_the_Sun",
    "sentence_index": 5,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "2ee104ccd06c2a90",
    "text": "Earth orbits the Sun at an average distance of about 149.6 million kilometres (93 million miles), taking 365.25 days to complete one revolution.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E2_Earth_The_Third_Planet_from_the_Sun.md",
    "document_id": "E2_Earth_The_Third_Planet_from_the_Sun",
    "sentence_index": 6,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "a293f93198a77e93",
    "text": "Its axial tilt of 23.44 degrees causes the annual seasons.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E2_Earth_The_Third_Planet_from_the_Sun.md",
    "document_id": "E2_Earth_The_Third_Planet_from_the_Sun",
    "sentence_index": 7,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "ac0475ba9bc20a19",
    "text": "The planet's surface is divided into tectonic plates that drift over geological time, creating continents and ocean basins.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E2_Earth_The_Third_Planet_from_the_Sun.md",
    "document_id": "E2_Earth_The_Third_Planet_from_the_Sun",
    "sentence_index": 8,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "18864f28996fc57a",
    "text": "Earth's Orbital and Physical Characteristics",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E3_Earths_Orbital_and_Physical_Characteris.md",
    "document_id": "E3_Earths_Orbital_and_Physical_Characteris",
    "sentence_index": 1,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "17fbeb682061eda9",
    "text": "Source: Wikipedia",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E3_Earths_Orbital_and_Physical_Characteris.md",
    "document_id": "E3_Earths_Orbital_and_Physical_Characteris",
    "sentence_index": 2,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "527bfbafb2e8d06b",
    "text": "Earth is about eight light-minutes away from the Sun, which means sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E3_Earths_Orbital_and_Physical_Characteris.md",
    "document_id": "E3_Earths_Orbital_and_Physical_Characteris",
    "sentence_index": 3,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "be55d68bf95d99e9",
    "text": "The planet has a moderately eccentric orbit (eccentricity 0.0167), making the distance to the Sun vary slightly over the year.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E3_Earths_Orbital_and_Physical_Characteris.md",
    "document_id": "E3_Earths_Orbital_and_Physical_Characteris",
    "sentence_index": 4,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "3fe84f9853d7bbfc",
    "text": "Earth's age is estimated at 4.54 billion years.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E3_Earths_Orbital_and_Physical_Characteris.md",
    "document_id": "E3_Earths_Orbital_and_Physical_Characteris",
    "sentence_index": 5,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "050c352ba9cfaaf9",
    "text": "The planet's atmosphere is composed mainly of nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%), which supports life.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E3_Earths_Orbital_and_Physical_Characteris.md",
    "document_id": "E3_Earths_Orbital_and_Physical_Characteris",
    "sentence_index": 6,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "f8a3e439ec2a7b98",
    "text": "Earth's magnetic field protects the surface from solar wind and cosmic radiation.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E3_Earths_Orbital_and_Physical_Characteris.md",
    "document_id": "E3_Earths_Orbital_and_Physical_Characteris",
    "sentence_index": 7,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "e4178ae0189914d1",
    "text": "The presence of liquid water, a stable climate, and a protective magnetic field make Earth uniquely habitable.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E3_Earths_Orbital_and_Physical_Characteris.md",
    "document_id": "E3_Earths_Orbital_and_Physical_Characteris",
    "sentence_index": 8,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "09ecfbec2bc8c19c",
    "text": "Formation and Evolution of the Solar System",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E4_Formation_and_Evolution_of_the_Solar_Sys.md",
    "document_id": "E4_Formation_and_Evolution_of_the_Solar_Sys",
    "sentence_index": 1,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "bdb26540dd531461",
    "text": "Source: Wikipedia",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E4_Formation_and_Evolution_of_the_Solar_Sys.md",
    "document_id": "E4_Formation_and_Evolution_of_the_Solar_Sys",
    "sentence_index": 2,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "4b56afa915c077c9",
    "text": "The Solar System formed about 4.6 billion years ago when a dense region of a molecular cloud collapsed under its own gravity.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E4_Formation_and_Evolution_of_the_Solar_Sys.md",
    "document_id": "E4_Formation_and_Evolution_of_the_Solar_Sys",
    "sentence_index": 3,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "aa8f38cdd24a0c77",
    "text": "The collapse likely was triggered by a shock wave from a nearby supernova.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E4_Formation_and_Evolution_of_the_Solar_Sys.md",
    "document_id": "E4_Formation_and_Evolution_of_the_Solar_Sys",
    "sentence_index": 4,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "c69b3045b469f9e1",
    "text": "The central concentration became the Sun, while the surrounding material flattened into a protoplanetary disc.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E4_Formation_and_Evolution_of_the_Solar_Sys.md",
    "document_id": "E4_Formation_and_Evolution_of_the_Solar_Sys",
    "sentence_index": 5,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "2a41afd332b8ab5a",
    "text": "Planetesimals -- small bodies of rock and ice -- formed and collided, gradually accreting into larger bodies.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E4_Formation_and_Evolution_of_the_Solar_Sys.md",
    "document_id": "E4_Formation_and_Evolution_of_the_Solar_Sys",
    "sentence_index": 6,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "2f77a765e9138f30",
    "text": "Within the first few million years, the giant planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) formed, and their gravitational influence shaped the orbits of the remaining bodies.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E4_Formation_and_Evolution_of_the_Solar_Sys.md",
    "document_id": "E4_Formation_and_Evolution_of_the_Solar_Sys",
    "sentence_index": 7,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "79ee9f37f9e5b02c",
    "text": "The Late Heavy Bombardment, about 4 billion years ago, delivered water and organic molecules to the inner planets, possibly seeding life on Earth.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E4_Formation_and_Evolution_of_the_Solar_Sys.md",
    "document_id": "E4_Formation_and_Evolution_of_the_Solar_Sys",
    "sentence_index": 8,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "ed89617434a7b820",
    "text": "Classification of Planets in the Solar System",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E5_Classification_of_Planets_in_the_Solar_S.md",
    "document_id": "E5_Classification_of_Planets_in_the_Solar_S",
    "sentence_index": 1,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "36af4fe7a6ff14fe",
    "text": "Source: Wikipedia",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E5_Classification_of_Planets_in_the_Solar_S.md",
    "document_id": "E5_Classification_of_Planets_in_the_Solar_S",
    "sentence_index": 2,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "7e732da471549371",
    "text": "The International Astronomical Union (IAU) defines a planet as a celestial body that: (1) orbits the Sun, (2) has sufficient mass for its self-gravity to overcome rigid body forces, assuming a nearly round shape, and (3) has cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E5_Classification_of_Planets_in_the_Solar_S.md",
    "document_id": "E5_Classification_of_Planets_in_the_Solar_S",
    "sentence_index": 3,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "59ed0e0d30ee2f5f",
    "text": "Based on this definition, there are eight planets:",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E5_Classification_of_Planets_in_the_Solar_S.md",
    "document_id": "E5_Classification_of_Planets_in_the_Solar_S",
    "sentence_index": 4,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "0577125f73157f21",
    "text": "Terrestrial planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E5_Classification_of_Planets_in_the_Solar_S.md",
    "document_id": "E5_Classification_of_Planets_in_the_Solar_S",
    "sentence_index": 5,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "c0fd3f58370ee716",
    "text": "Gas giants: Jupiter, Saturn.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E5_Classification_of_Planets_in_the_Solar_S.md",
    "document_id": "E5_Classification_of_Planets_in_the_Solar_S",
    "sentence_index": 6,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "882abc5b43f37a07",
    "text": "Ice giants: Uranus, Neptune.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E5_Classification_of_Planets_in_the_Solar_S.md",
    "document_id": "E5_Classification_of_Planets_in_the_Solar_S",
    "sentence_index": 7,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "78389dd7d867dd1b",
    "text": "Pluto, Eris, Haumea, Makemake, and Ceres are classified as dwarf planets.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E5_Classification_of_Planets_in_the_Solar_S.md",
    "document_id": "E5_Classification_of_Planets_in_the_Solar_S",
    "sentence_index": 8,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "910ec46a5a7752d4",
    "text": "The Solar System also contains hundreds of thousands of asteroids, comets, and many moons.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E5_Classification_of_Planets_in_the_Solar_S.md",
    "document_id": "E5_Classification_of_Planets_in_the_Solar_S",
    "sentence_index": 9,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "2b471b982e5ccc85",
    "text": "Earth's Density and Mass",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E6_Earths_Density_and_Mass.md",
    "document_id": "E6_Earths_Density_and_Mass",
    "sentence_index": 1,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "5837b84329439142",
    "text": "Source: Wikipedia",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E6_Earths_Density_and_Mass.md",
    "document_id": "E6_Earths_Density_and_Mass",
    "sentence_index": 2,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "f0d963af13913af8",
    "text": "Earth is the densest planet in the Solar System, with an average density of 5.51 g/cm3.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E6_Earths_Density_and_Mass.md",
    "document_id": "E6_Earths_Density_and_Mass",
    "sentence_index": 3,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "3f2bf521d3112638",
    "text": "This high density is due to its metallic core, which is composed mainly of iron and nickel.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E6_Earths_Density_and_Mass.md",
    "document_id": "E6_Earths_Density_and_Mass",
    "sentence_index": 4,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "8cb85cecb649ccb3",
    "text": "Of the four rocky planets, Earth is the largest and most massive.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E6_Earths_Density_and_Mass.md",
    "document_id": "E6_Earths_Density_and_Mass",
    "sentence_index": 5,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "783de26571ae43ab",
    "text": "Earth's near-surface environments are the only places in the universe known to harbour life.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E6_Earths_Density_and_Mass.md",
    "document_id": "E6_Earths_Density_and_Mass",
    "sentence_index": 6,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "efb92d3b21601295",
    "text": "Its atmosphere, hydrosphere, and lithosphere interact in complex cycles that maintain a habitable climate.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E6_Earths_Density_and_Mass.md",
    "document_id": "E6_Earths_Density_and_Mass",
    "sentence_index": 7,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "3b6bc2123e232270",
    "text": "The existence of plate tectonics and a magnetic field are believed to be critical for sustaining life over geological time.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E6_Earths_Density_and_Mass.md",
    "document_id": "E6_Earths_Density_and_Mass",
    "sentence_index": 8,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "753e0f397b8ae9b1",
    "text": "The Sun's Dominance in the Solar System",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E7_The_Suns_Dominance_in_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E7_The_Suns_Dominance_in_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 1,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "82fecf60aebbf2df",
    "text": "Source: Wikipedia",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E7_The_Suns_Dominance_in_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E7_The_Suns_Dominance_in_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 2,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "b99881e506560a53",
    "text": "Over 99.86% of the Solar System's mass is located within the Sun.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E7_The_Suns_Dominance_in_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E7_The_Suns_Dominance_in_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 3,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "690e454475b322dc",
    "text": "The Sun is a G-type main-sequence star that fuses hydrogen into helium in its core.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E7_The_Suns_Dominance_in_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E7_The_Suns_Dominance_in_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 4,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "9867149b96fe8333",
    "text": "Its gravitational pull holds the entire system together, dictating the orbits of all planets, asteroids, and comets.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E7_The_Suns_Dominance_in_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E7_The_Suns_Dominance_in_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 5,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "3d17e0a216b2cce1",
    "text": "The Sun's energy output, known as solar luminosity, is the primary driver of climate and weather on Earth.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E7_The_Suns_Dominance_in_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E7_The_Suns_Dominance_in_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 6,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "ba8dc4146c8b7ec8",
    "text": "Solar activity, such as sunspots and solar flares, can affect space weather and have impacts on satellite operations and power grids.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E7_The_Suns_Dominance_in_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E7_The_Suns_Dominance_in_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 7,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "e259e29e3d61d0d4",
    "text": "Understanding the Sun is crucial for understanding the Solar System's past, present, and future.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E7_The_Suns_Dominance_in_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E7_The_Suns_Dominance_in_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 8,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "6881fac168de6fd6",
    "text": "Boundaries and Structure of the Solar System",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E8_Boundaries_and_Structure_of_the_Solar_Sy.md",
    "document_id": "E8_Boundaries_and_Structure_of_the_Solar_Sy",
    "sentence_index": 1,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "760dcda0be7870be",
    "text": "Source: Wikipedia",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E8_Boundaries_and_Structure_of_the_Solar_Sy.md",
    "document_id": "E8_Boundaries_and_Structure_of_the_Solar_Sy",
    "sentence_index": 2,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "8041cdd3e9ede542",
    "text": "The Solar System's boundaries are defined by several markers:",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E8_Boundaries_and_Structure_of_the_Solar_Sy.md",
    "document_id": "E8_Boundaries_and_Structure_of_the_Solar_Sy",
    "sentence_index": 3,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "60400f4f252d0bd5",
    "text": "Kuiper Belt: A region beyond Neptune containing many icy bodies, extending from about 30 to 50 AU.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E8_Boundaries_and_Structure_of_the_Solar_Sy.md",
    "document_id": "E8_Boundaries_and_Structure_of_the_Solar_Sy",
    "sentence_index": 4,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "dad9de74a1bb898d",
    "text": "Kuiper Cliff: A sudden drop in the number of objects at about 50 AU, possibly indicating the edge of the Kuiper Belt.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E8_Boundaries_and_Structure_of_the_Solar_Sy.md",
    "document_id": "E8_Boundaries_and_Structure_of_the_Solar_Sy",
    "sentence_index": 5,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "0b771244793e094b",
    "text": "Heliopause: The boundary where the solar wind meets the interstellar medium, located at about 120 AU.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E8_Boundaries_and_Structure_of_the_Solar_Sy.md",
    "document_id": "E8_Boundaries_and_Structure_of_the_Solar_Sy",
    "sentence_index": 6,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "de97bfedf8c0bb53",
    "text": "Beyond this lies the Oort Cloud, a spherical reservoir of comets extending up to 100,000 AU.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E8_Boundaries_and_Structure_of_the_Solar_Sy.md",
    "document_id": "E8_Boundaries_and_Structure_of_the_Solar_Sy",
    "sentence_index": 7,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "188f8cab94ff9b17",
    "text": "The termination shock, the heliosheath, and the heliopause are the main features of the heliosphere -- the bubble blown by the solar wind into the interstellar medium.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E8_Boundaries_and_Structure_of_the_Solar_Sy.md",
    "document_id": "E8_Boundaries_and_Structure_of_the_Solar_Sy",
    "sentence_index": 8,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "04bc66e8e77248db",
    "text": "The boundary structures define the zone influenced by the Sun's magnetic field and solar wind.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E8_Boundaries_and_Structure_of_the_Solar_Sy.md",
    "document_id": "E8_Boundaries_and_Structure_of_the_Solar_Sy",
    "sentence_index": 9,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "858c76711d74d0f5",
    "text": "Minor Bodies in the Solar System",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E9_Minor_Bodies_in_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E9_Minor_Bodies_in_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 1,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "0ab82bc0c7b61270",
    "text": "Source: Wikipedia",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E9_Minor_Bodies_in_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E9_Minor_Bodies_in_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 2,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "d3b755db56367453",
    "text": "The Solar System contains a vast number of minor bodies:",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E9_Minor_Bodies_in_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E9_Minor_Bodies_in_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 3,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "4d055df2ba7e95e7",
    "text": "Minor planets: Known count as of 2026 is about 1,368,528, with the vast majority being asteroids in the main belt between Mars and Jupiter.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E9_Minor_Bodies_in_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E9_Minor_Bodies_in_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 4,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "44ced360833e64a5",
    "text": "Comets: About 4,591 known comets, including both short-period and long-period comets.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E9_Minor_Bodies_in_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E9_Minor_Bodies_in_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 5,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "4ca6463ccc5d7716",
    "text": "Natural satellites: 758 known moons orbiting planets and dwarf planets.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E9_Minor_Bodies_in_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E9_Minor_Bodies_in_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 6,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "e34abf213cf38c5c",
    "text": "These minor bodies provide valuable clues about the early Solar System, as they have preserved much of the original material from the protoplanetary disc.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E9_Minor_Bodies_in_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E9_Minor_Bodies_in_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 7,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  },
  {
    "claim_id": "f5f8c38c6c0ac289",
    "text": "They are also objects of interest for future exploration, resource extraction, and as potential impact hazards.",
    "source_path": "C:\\Projects\\SMRITI\\smriti\\data\\raw\\gold_vault\\E9_Minor_Bodies_in_the_Solar_System.md",
    "document_id": "E9_Minor_Bodies_in_the_Solar_System",
    "sentence_index": 8,
    "method": "naive_keyword_baseline"
  }
]
````

## File: evaluation/controlled/score_controlled.py
````python
"""
score_controlled.py — Score SMRITI against SMRITI-Controlled-v1's gold manifest.

Unlike evaluation/annotation/score.py, this needs NO annotation pass at all:
the gold_manifest.json IS the ground truth, by construction (every pair was
written to have an unambiguous, objective relationship — numeric facts,
explicit negation, named-entity attribution). This directly measures both
RETRIEVAL recall (did the intended pair even become an NLI candidate?) and
CLASSIFICATION accuracy (given it was retrieved, was it labeled correctly?)
separately, per the review's P1-13 recommendation.

Run with: poetry run python evaluation/controlled/score_controlled.py <run_id>
"""
import json
import os
import sys
from collections import defaultdict

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(r"C:\Projects\SMRITI\smriti", "src"))
from smriti.evaluation.statistical.bootstrap import bootstrap_proportion_ci

BASE = r"C:\Projects\SMRITI\smriti"
MANIFEST_PATH = os.path.join(BASE, "evaluation", "controlled", "gold_manifest.json")


def doc_id_from_path(path: str) -> str:
    return os.path.basename(path).replace(".md", "")


def main(run_id: str):
    art = os.path.join(BASE, "artifacts", f"run_{run_id}")
    p4 = json.load(open(os.path.join(art, "phase4", "dataset.json"), encoding="utf-8"))
    p6 = json.load(open(os.path.join(art, "phase6", "dataset.json"), encoding="utf-8"))
    manifest = json.load(open(MANIFEST_PATH, encoding="utf-8"))

    doc_of_claim = {c["claim_id"]: doc_id_from_path(c["source_path"]) for c in p4}
    claim_of_doc = {v: k for k, v in doc_of_claim.items()}  # 1 claim per doc in this corpus

    predicted_by_pair = {}
    for r in p6:
        a, b = r["claim_id_a"], r["claim_id_b"]
        key = frozenset([doc_of_claim.get(a), doc_of_claim.get(b)])
        predicted_by_pair[key] = r["relationship_type"].upper()

    per_category = defaultdict(lambda: {"retrieved": 0, "total": 0, "correct": 0})
    rows = []
    for pair in manifest:
        key = frozenset([pair["doc_a"], pair["doc_b"]])
        gold = pair["gold_relationship"]
        category = pair["category"]
        predicted = predicted_by_pair.get(key)
        retrieved = predicted is not None
        correct = retrieved and predicted == gold

        per_category[category]["total"] += 1
        if retrieved:
            per_category[category]["retrieved"] += 1
        if correct:
            per_category[category]["correct"] += 1

        rows.append({
            "pair": f"{pair['doc_a']}/{pair['doc_b']}",
            "gold": gold, "category": category,
            "retrieved": retrieved, "predicted": predicted, "correct": correct,
        })

    print(f"{'Category':<12} {'Total':>6} {'Retrieved':>10} {'RetrievalRecall':>16} {'CorrectGivenRetrieved':>22} {'ClassAccuracy':>14}")
    overall = {"total": 0, "retrieved": 0, "correct": 0}
    for cat, d in sorted(per_category.items()):
        recall = d["retrieved"] / d["total"] if d["total"] else 0.0
        class_acc = d["correct"] / d["retrieved"] if d["retrieved"] else 0.0
        overall["total"] += d["total"]
        overall["retrieved"] += d["retrieved"]
        overall["correct"] += d["correct"]
        print(f"{cat:<12} {d['total']:>6} {d['retrieved']:>10} {recall:>16.1%} {d['correct']:>10}/{d['retrieved']:<10} {class_acc:>14.1%}")

    print("-" * 90)
    overall_recall = overall["retrieved"] / overall["total"] if overall["total"] else 0.0
    overall_class_acc = overall["correct"] / overall["retrieved"] if overall["retrieved"] else 0.0
    print(f"{'TOTAL':<12} {overall['total']:>6} {overall['retrieved']:>10} {overall_recall:>16.1%} "
          f"{overall['correct']:>10}/{overall['retrieved']:<10} {overall_class_acc:>14.1%}")

    # ── Bootstrap 95% CIs (P1-11): sampling uncertainty, not run-to-run noise ──
    retrieval_outcomes = [r["retrieved"] for r in rows]
    classification_outcomes = [r["correct"] for r in rows if r["retrieved"]]
    recall_ci = bootstrap_proportion_ci(retrieval_outcomes)
    class_acc_ci = bootstrap_proportion_ci(classification_outcomes) if classification_outcomes else None
    print(f"\nRetrieval recall 95% CI:        {recall_ci.point_estimate:.1%} "
          f"[{recall_ci.ci_lower:.1%}, {recall_ci.ci_upper:.1%}] (n={recall_ci.n_items})")
    if class_acc_ci:
        print(f"Classification accuracy 95% CI: {class_acc_ci.point_estimate:.1%} "
              f"[{class_acc_ci.ci_lower:.1%}, {class_acc_ci.ci_upper:.1%}] (n={class_acc_ci.n_items})")

    out = {
        "run_id": run_id,
        "per_category": {k: dict(v) for k, v in per_category.items()},
        "overall": overall,
        "overall_retrieval_recall": round(overall_recall, 4),
        "overall_classification_accuracy_given_retrieved": round(overall_class_acc, 4),
        "retrieval_recall_bootstrap_ci": vars(recall_ci),
        "classification_accuracy_bootstrap_ci": vars(class_acc_ci) if class_acc_ci else None,
        "rows": rows,
    }
    out_path = os.path.join(BASE, "evaluation", "controlled", "results.json")
    json.dump(out, open(out_path, "w", encoding="utf-8"), indent=2)
    print(f"\nWritten to {out_path}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_id = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "20260909_193916"
    main(run_id)
````

## File: paper/sections/ablation.tex
````latex
We run a leave-one-signal-out ablation (P1-6/P1-7) against the real,
post-fix 215-claim SMRITI-Reference scoring run reported in
\S\ref{sec:metamorphic}'s reconstruction test: for each of Phase 8's
seven registered signals, we zero that signal's policy weight
\emph{without} renormalizing the remaining six, re-score every claim
through the real, unmodified fusion code, and compare against the
all-signals baseline. Zeroing rather than renormalizing isolates exactly
that signal's own contribution, consistent with standard leave-one-out
sensitivity analysis; the code and full per-signal results are released
(\texttt{evaluation/ablation/run\_ablation.py}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
\textbf{Signal} & \textbf{Weight} & \textbf{Mean shift} & $r$ \\
\midrule
topology\_strength     & 0.10 & $-1.81$ & 0.954 \\
temporal\_stability     & 0.05 & $-1.31$ & 0.993 \\
conflict\_pressure      & 0.20 & $+1.31$ & 0.989 \\
evidence\_independence  & 0.15 & $-0.66$ & 0.971 \\
evidence\_strength      & 0.25 & $-0.61$ & 0.986 \\
bridge\_score           & 0.05 & $-0.40$ & 0.991 \\
source\_diversity       & 0.15 & $-0.22$ & 0.999 \\
hub\_score              & 0.05 & $-0.02$ & 0.999 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Effect of zeroing each signal's policy weight on the 215-claim
SMRITI-Reference reliability distribution (baseline mean
$\mathrm{RI}=4.99$/100). Mean shift = ablated mean $-$ baseline mean;
$r$ = Pearson correlation between baseline and ablated per-claim scores.
Ranked by mean absolute per-claim delta (Table order here follows that
ranking, most to least disruptive).}
\label{tab:ablation}
\end{table}

Two findings are worth stating plainly. \textbf{(1) The baseline mean
reliability index across all 215 claims is 4.99 out of 100} --- not a
property of the ablation, but of the corpus as currently scored, and
consistent with \S\ref{sec:error-taxonomy}'s finding that partition
fragmentation and widespread constraint firing (each ablation run logs
$\geq 1$ fired constraint for the large majority of claims) suppress
reliability system-wide; this table should be read as \emph{relative}
sensitivity, not as evidence that any individual signal is well-
calibrated in absolute terms. \textbf{(2) Policy weight does not predict
empirical sensitivity.} \texttt{topology\_strength} carries a policy
weight of only 0.10 --- less than half of \texttt{evidence\_strength}'s
0.25 --- yet removing it shifts the mean score three times as much
(and produces the lowest correlation with baseline, $r=0.954$, i.e.\ the
most rank-order disruption). This is not a bug: Phase 8's fusion applies
policy-level constraints and interactions on top of the raw weighted sum
(\S\ref{sec:system}) --- for instance a floor tied to topology under
\texttt{min\_reliability\_for\_high\_topology} --- so a signal's linear
weight is not the same quantity as its effect on the final,
constraint-adjusted score. \texttt{conflict\_pressure}'s positive mean
shift on removal ($+1.31$) is the expected sign check: it is the fusion's
only negative-direction signal, so removing its penalty raises scores,
consistent with \S\ref{sec:bugs} Defect 7's fix depending on this signal
being real and non-zero. \texttt{hub\_score} is, by a wide margin, the
least consequential signal in the current policy ($r=0.999$), a concrete
candidate for reweighting or removal in future policy tuning.
````

## File: paper/sections/annotation_protocol.tex
````latex
\paragraph{Why not human annotation, and why ``Reference'' not ``Gold''.}
A rigorous evaluation of extraction precision/recall and relationship-
classification accuracy benefits enormously from ground truth. Recruiting,
training, and adjudicating a panel of human annotators with measured
inter-annotator agreement was outside what could be produced for this
paper. We are explicit that what follows is \emph{not} a substitute for
that: it is a disclosed, LLM-derived reference annotation. We call the
corpus it labels ``SMRITI-Reference'', reserving ``Gold'' for a corpus with
externally human-labeled ground truth, which this is not. It is useful for
a first-pass quantitative signal and for detecting gross calibration
failures, but not sufficient on its own to certify SMRITI's real-world
accuracy. \S\ref{sec:limitations} states exactly what a follow-up human
study would need to add.

\paragraph{Protocol.} Two independent annotation passes (no shared
context, no access to SMRITI's own predictions or to each other's output)
are run over: (i) a stratified sample of claims with full coverage of
every claim touching a deliberately-contradictory document, judged for
\emph{validity} (is this a structurally sound claim, or extraction noise),
\emph{quality} (1--5), and \emph{reliability} (1--5, an epistemic-
credibility judgment independent of extraction quality); and (ii) a
stratified sample of relationship candidates, comprising every candidate
pair between a deliberately-contradictory document and its stated target,
a sample of candidate pairs between a deliberately-contradictory document
and an unrelated document (to measure spurious cross-domain contradiction
rate), and a stratified sample of SMRITI's other predicted relationship
types, labeled SUPPORTS / CONTRADICTS / REFINES / NEUTRAL / UNSURE.
Annotators are blind to SMRITI's own predicted labels throughout.

\paragraph{This annotation round was re-run from scratch.} The claim- and
relationship-extraction fixes described in \S\ref{sec:system} (the
assertion classifier and the resolver arg-max/relatedness-gate fix) change
which claims and candidate pairs SMRITI produces at all, so a reference
annotation collected before those fixes would be scored against a
population of claims and pairs that no longer exists. We therefore
re-sampled and re-annotated against the corrected system's output rather
than reusing the pre-fix annotation; both rounds' raw data are released for
inspection.
````

## File: paper/sections/annotation_results.tex
````latex
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
\textbf{Task} & \textbf{Inter-pass agreement} & \textbf{N} \\
\midrule
Claim validity (binary) & $\kappa=0.987$ & 300 \\
Claim reliability (1--5) & MAD $=0.15$ & 296 \\
Relationship type (5-way) & $\kappa=0.675$ & 310 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Inter-pass agreement between the two independent LLM-derived
annotation passes. $\kappa$ = Cohen's kappa; MAD = mean absolute difference
on the 1--5 scale. Per Landis and Koch's conventional bands, claim validity
agreement is \emph{almost perfect} and relationship-type agreement is
\emph{substantial} but below the $\kappa > 0.7$ bar typically required
before treating labels as reliable ground truth --- itself evidence that even
holding the annotator (an LLM under a fixed protocol) constant, relationship
typing is a harder, more subjective task than validity judgment, and this
should be read as a lower bound on how much harder it would be across two
\emph{different human} annotators.}
\label{tab:agreement}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Claim extraction (RC1).} On the 298 claims where both annotation
passes agreed on validity (99.3\% of the sample), only 54.0\% were judged
structurally valid claims --- sharply lower than the value SMRITI's own
built-in Phase 12 evaluation reports for the analogous check (which treats
any \emph{non-empty} extracted span as ``precise'' and reports effectively
100\%). Directly inspecting the full 726-claim Phase 4 output confirms why:
7.3\% of all extracted claims are pure bibliographic metadata lines (e.g.\ a
``\textbf{Source:}'' attribution) with no assertional content at all, and a
further substantial fraction are bare headings, ingredient-list noun
phrases, or dangling sentence fragments from imperfect sentence
segmentation. \textbf{We could not measure recall} for claim extraction
with this protocol --- doing so requires an annotator to read each source
document in full and enumerate every assertable claim, independent of
what SMRITI extracted, which is a substantially larger annotation task we
did not undertake; we flag this explicitly as unmeasured rather than
estimating it.

\paragraph{Relationship classification (RC2/RC3).} Table~\ref{tab:relprf1}
reports SMRITI's own per-class precision/recall/F1 against the 269
relationship pairs where both annotation passes agreed (excluding UNSURE).
The result is stark: SMRITI's NLI-based classifier achieves reasonable
NEUTRAL-class performance (F1 $=0.593$) but its CONTRADICTS precision is
only \textbf{3.2\%} --- of every candidate pair SMRITI labeled CONTRADICTS in
this sample, 96.8\% were judged NOT to be genuine contradictions by both
independent annotation passes. Recall on the 68 held-out pairs drawn from
the corpus's deliberately-planted, known-answer contradiction set
(hard-contradiction target pairs, \S\ref{sec:corpus}) is only
\textbf{25.0\%} --- SMRITI correctly flags just one in four of the
contradictions the corpus was specifically constructed to contain. Precision
and recall being simultaneously this low on the same label is the
signature of a classifier whose CONTRADICTS predictions are close to
uncorrelated with the true contradiction structure, not merely
miscalibrated in one direction; \S\ref{sec:error-analysis} traces this to
out-of-distribution NLI behavior on embedding-retrieved candidate pairs.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}
\toprule
\textbf{Class} & \textbf{P} & \textbf{R} & \textbf{F1} & \textbf{N} \\
\midrule
SUPPORTS     & 0.100 & 0.143 & 0.118 & 28 \\
CONTRADICTS  & 0.032 & 0.286 & 0.057 & 7 \\
REFINES      & 0.122 & 0.333 & 0.179 & 15 \\
NEUTRAL      & 0.816 & 0.466 & 0.593 & 219 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{SMRITI's relationship classification, scored against the
annotator-agreed subset ($N=269$). Support column is the number of
gold-labeled instances of that class in the agreed subset.}
\label{tab:relprf1}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Baseline comparison.} Table~\ref{tab:baseline-comparison} compares
SMRITI's NLI classifier against both baselines on the identical agreed-gold
subset. The result is counter-intuitive and, we think, important: the
\emph{naive} TF-IDF cosine baseline achieves \textbf{perfect CONTRADICTS
precision (1.00)} on this sample (every pair it labeled CONTRADICTS was a
genuine contradiction), far exceeding SMRITI's 0.032 --- though at much lower
recall (0.143 vs.\ SMRITI's 0.286), since TF-IDF's shallow negation-cue
heuristic is far more conservative about calling CONTRADICTS at all. The
Sentence-BERT baseline sits between the two (CONTRADICTS precision 0.50).
Neither baseline handles REFINES at all (F1 $=0$ for both), which is
unsurprising since neither implements any structural notion of
elaboration/narrowing beyond similarity-band thresholds. \textbf{No system
in this comparison is good enough to deploy as-is}: SMRITI over-predicts
CONTRADICTS with very low precision, and both baselines are simply too
conservative on it to be useful for the contradiction-detection use case
that motivates SMRITI's design in the first place. We read this as evidence
that off-the-shelf sentence-similarity-thresholded heuristics and
off-the-shelf NLI models are \emph{both} the wrong tool for this exact task
without further adaptation --- a concrete, falsifiable target for future work
rather than a reason to prefer one architecture over the other.
````

## File: paper/sections/bugs.tex
````latex
Running the full pipeline against SMRITI-Reference --- rather than the
small, hand-crafted fixtures used in the existing unit test suite ---
surfaced three defects that had not been previously detected, all directly
attributable to properties the corpus was designed to exercise. A
subsequent audit of the system's own evaluation and reliability layers,
motivated by an external review, surfaced four more.

\paragraph{Defect 1: console encoding crash on non-ASCII input.} SMRITI's
structured logger wrote to the process's default console stream without
specifying an encoding. On Windows, this stream defaults to a legacy
single-byte codepage (e.g.\ cp1252), which cannot encode most non-Latin
scripts. Any log line containing non-Latin script text --- for example, the
Kannada conjunct-consonant examples in the corpus's B7/B8 documents ---
raised an unhandled \texttt{UnicodeEncodeError} that crashed the entire
pipeline run --- not a degraded result, a hard failure that made the system
entirely unusable on this input. The fix reconfigures both the standard-
library logging stream handler and the interpreter's raw
\texttt{stdout}/\texttt{stderr} streams to UTF-8 with
\texttt{errors="backslashreplace"}. This defect would not have been found
on an English-only test corpus; it required a real multi-script document.

\paragraph{Defect 2: contradiction leakage under odd contradiction
cycles.} Phase 7's constraint-based partitioning algorithm
(\S\ref{sec:phase7}) 2-colors the contradiction-only subgraph via
breadth-first search. When a connected component of the contradiction
subgraph is \emph{not} bipartite (an odd contradiction cycle), the original
BFS coloring routine detected the conflict and returned failure, but only
\emph{after} already writing partial, inconsistent colors into the shared
color map for every node it had visited before the conflicting edge was
reached, so the intended ``degrade to singletons'' fallback silently left
some nodes with unvalidated colors. On SMRITI-Reference, this manifested
as a hard \texttt{PartitioningError} once independently-contradicting
claim clusters (themselves a symptom of the original contradiction
over-firing described in \S\ref{sec:error-analysis}) happened to form an
odd cycle --- something a small test fixture with one contradicting pair
cannot trigger. The fix isolates each 2-coloring attempt in a scratch
dictionary local to its connected component, committing to the shared map
only on full success.

\paragraph{Defect 3: uninitialized variable and misplaced phase-7 call in
the pipeline runner.} A latent bug in \texttt{PipelineRunner.run} left the
\texttt{phase4\_claims} variable unassigned when resuming a run starting
at Phase 7 or later, raising an \texttt{UnboundLocalError} on any
partial-resume invocation past Phase 6 --- a code path the existing tests,
which always start from Phase 1, never exercised. A second, adjacent
indentation error caused the call to \texttt{\_run\_phase\_7} to execute
unconditionally regardless of the requested phase range. Both are fixed.

All three fixes are behavior-preserving for every phase-range
configuration already covered by the unit test suite and are exercised
end-to-end by the SMRITI-Reference runs reported in \S\ref{sec:results}.

\paragraph{Defect 4: the system's own evaluation layer fabricated
evidence.} Described at length in \S\ref{sec:cleanup}: Phase 12's prior
implementation computed a claim-extraction ``precision'' as
non-emptiness, an invented ``recall'' with no relationship to any missed
claim, a hard-coded ``generalization confidence'' of 50.0 regardless of
what was measured, and a ``statistical support'' score that rewarded
registering more experiments rather than finding anything. We classify
this as a defect, not merely a limitation, because it actively produced a
misleadingly high confidence number (an earlier Scientific Confidence
Index of 57.0/100) that a reader could mistake for evidence.

\paragraph{Defect 5: the relationship resolver never checked the
dominant NLI class.} The root cause of the 3.2\% CONTRADICTS precision
this paper's predecessor measured (\S\ref{sec:error-analysis}): the
resolver's CONTRADICTS rule required only \texttt{contradiction\_score >
entailment\_score} by a margin, never comparing against
\texttt{neutral\_score}. A pair where neutral was the model's actual
dominant class (e.g.\ contradiction $=0.85$, entailment $=0.05$, neutral
$=0.90$) still resolved to CONTRADICTS. Fixed in \S\ref{sec:system} by
requiring the winning class to be the genuine arg-max of all three scores.

\paragraph{Defect 6: evidence independence rewarded the absence of
evidence.} The evidence-independence signal extractor
(\texttt{scoring/signals/independence.py}) returned its \emph{maximum}
value (1.0, ``fully independent'') whenever a claim had zero supporting
evidence --- literally: no evidence to evaluate became maximum independence.
Fixed to return \texttt{UNAVAILABLE} with value 0.0, so a claim with
nothing to evaluate no longer receives a positive contribution from a
signal that had nothing real to measure (\S\ref{sec:system}).

\paragraph{Test suite health.} Separately from the defects above, we found
the suite carrying 80 failing tests at the start of this work --- stale-
fixture drift plus a handful of genuine, previously-undetected production
bugs of the same character as Defect 3, including one config file
silently overriding every policy-profile selection with a hardcoded value,
and one code path where a sentence's coordinated-object structure
(``Python supports generators and decorators'') was not distinguished
from coordinated-clause structure. All 80 were fixed without weakening any
assertion.

\paragraph{Defect 7: uncertainty score blind to conflict pressure.}
\texttt{uncertainty\_score} and \texttt{reliability\_index} are reported as
two distinct metrics, but \texttt{\_compute\_uncertainty()}
(\texttt{scoring/fusion.py}) combined only evidence-sufficiency components
(incompleteness, low source diversity, low independence) and never read
\texttt{conflict\_pressure} at all. A claim under heavy, active dispute
therefore registered a correctly-lowered reliability but an
\emph{unchanged} uncertainty score --- the metric meant to answer ``how
much should a reader trust this number'' did not move even when the honest
answer was ``much less, it is contested.'' Fixed by adding
\texttt{conflict\_pressure} as a fourth weighted uncertainty component;
verified directly by metamorphic relation MR2 (\S\ref{sec:metamorphic}),
which now asserts uncertainty strictly increases under contradiction, not
only that reliability does not increase.

\paragraph{Defect 8: dashboard views bypassing the Command layer.}
SMRITI's Phase 10 dashboard architecture requires that views communicate
user actions to state via typed \texttt{Command} objects dispatched
through an \texttt{InteractionDispatcher}, never by calling state-mutating
methods directly. Two views (\texttt{NavigationView},
\texttt{ResultListView}) violated this by importing the concrete
\texttt{EpistemicStateManager} class directly (caught by an existing but
previously-failing static dependency-matrix test) and calling
\texttt{navigate\_back()}/\texttt{select\_claim()}/\texttt{set\_page()}
directly. Both are fixed to follow the same dispatcher-based pattern
already used correctly by \texttt{SearchView}, with new unit tests added
since neither view had prior coverage.
````

## File: paper/sections/conclusion.tex
````latex
This paper is, in a specific sense, a paper about being wrong and then
checking the work. Its predecessor built genuine engineering rigor ---
phase-isolated boundaries, full provenance, reproducible manifests --- and
then measured its own scientific claims with a self-evaluation layer that,
on inspection, was not measuring what it claimed to. The corrective
process was not cosmetic: deleting the fabricated metrics did not, by
itself, fix anything --- it only stopped hiding that the underlying
relationship classifier had a 3.2\% CONTRADICTS precision. Finding and
fixing \emph{that} required reading the resolver code line by line and
noticing it never checked the neutral score. The fix is one function; the
evidence that it generalizes required building a corpus specifically
designed to need no interpretation at all.

Three things now stand on genuinely independent legs. SMRITI-Controlled
(\S\ref{sec:controlled}) shows 100\% CONTRADICTS classification accuracy
on every retrieved pair across six distinct contradiction categories, with
zero false positives on six deliberately unrelated control pairs --- by
construction, not by annotation. The metamorphic and reconstruction tests
(\S\ref{sec:metamorphic}) show the reliability model is not
self-contradictory in basic, checkable ways, and that its audit trail
means what it says. And the re-run SMRITI-Reference annotation
(\S\ref{sec:results-annotation}) gives the fourth leg a very different
shape than the other three: it does not confirm the fix's real-world
value, it discloses the fix's real-world limit. CONTRADICTS precision on
SMRITI-Reference's actual prose is 4.6\%, statistically no better than
the 3.2\% measured before any of this paper's fixes, because the corpus's
genuine disagreements are argued rhetorically, not asserted
propositionally, and an off-the-shelf entailment model simply does not
hear rhetoric as contradiction. We could have stopped at
SMRITI-Controlled's 100\% and called the story finished; re-running the
annotation after the fix, rather than reusing the pre-fix round, is what
surfaced that it was not.

What does not yet stand on solid ground is explicitly listed in
\S\ref{sec:limitations}, not hidden in a "future work" paragraph few
readers reach: the resolver fix does not transfer to rhetorical
disagreement in real text, SUPPORTS classification is still weak on both
corpora, source-diversity and temporal signals still rest on filesystem
heuristics rather than real provenance, and no genuine human evaluation
exists. We release SMRITI-Reference, SMRITI-Controlled, both annotation
rounds, the scoring code, and the fixed system itself, so that closing
those gaps --- including, eventually, the human validation study we could
not ourselves produce, and a genuinely stance-aware relationship
classifier --- starts from a system that has already been checked once,
rather than one whose self-report has to be checked first.
````

## File: paper/sections/controlled_corpus.tex
````latex
\section{SMRITI-Controlled: A Zero-Annotation Evaluation}
\label{sec:controlled}

SMRITI-Reference's contradiction pairs (\S\ref{sec:corpus}), while
deliberately planted, still involve claims about ML architectures,
cricket tactics, and cooking technique --- domains where a human or LLM
annotator's judgment of ``does this really contradict that'' still
requires interpretation. To obtain evidence that requires \emph{no}
interpretation at all, we construct SMRITI-Controlled-v1: 24 claim pairs
(48 single-sentence documents), each written so its relationship label is
a fact about how the pair was constructed, not an opinion about what it
means. Six categories of CONTRADICTS pairs (2 each): \emph{direct}
reversal ("uses 4 GB of RAM" vs.\ "uses 8 GB of RAM"), \emph{negated}
("supports GPU execution" vs.\ "does not support GPU execution"),
\emph{numeric} ("Jupiter has 95 known moons" vs.\ "79 known moons"),
\emph{temporal} (same explicit time reference, opposite state),
\emph{entity} (same artifact attributed to two different named
individuals/teams), and \emph{attribute} (a property asserted and its
negation). We add 6 SUPPORTS pairs (a claim and an independent
confirmation of the same claim) and 6 NEUTRAL pairs (entirely unrelated
topics) as controls. The full corpus and its gold manifest are released.

Because the label is definitional, we can additionally separate
\textbf{retrieval recall} (did the intended pair even become an NLI
candidate?) from \textbf{classification accuracy} (given it was a
candidate, was it labeled correctly?) --- the distinction the review
identified as necessary to know whether SMRITI's bottleneck is
embedding-based retrieval or NLI classification.

\input{sections/controlled_results.tex}
````
